Text: {{c1::Therapeutic communication::approach}} uses both {{c2::verbal}} and {{c2::nonverbal}} techniques to encourage patients to {{c3::express how they are feeling}} and to achieve a {{c3::positive relationship}} with the patient.
Back Extra:
Ex: Nonverbal channels include eye contact, body position, and facial expressions.

Cue: Factors like age, culture, environment, and voice tempo all shape how a message is received.
coverage_notes: Definition note: c1 = the term, c2 = the verbal+nonverbal qualifier, c3 = the two goals grouped as one cohesive pair (all three must-test facts clozed).

Text: {{c1::Tone}}, {{c1::pace}}, and {{c1::volume}} of speech — not just the words themselves — tell you about a patient's {{c2::mood}} and the perceived {{c2::importance}} of the message.
Back Extra: Pitfall: A yelling patient is not necessarily hostile — the patient may be angry, scared, or both.
coverage_notes: How-said highlight concretized as the tone/pace/volume triad from context; payoffs (mood, importance) clozed as c2.

Text: Direct eye contact conveys {{c1::honesty and respect::honesty and respect / confrontation}} in the United States and most European countries, but conveys {{c1::confrontation::honesty and respect / confrontation}} in Latin American, Asian, and African cultures.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: A patient who avoids your gaze may be showing politeness, not evasiveness — read the behavior through the patient's culture.

Distinguish: In some cultures the reverse rule holds — it is impolite to look away while someone is speaking.
coverage_notes: Comparison archetype: culture groups visible, differing meanings clozed under c1 with forced-choice hints.

Text: {{c1::Ethnocentrism::ethnocentrism / cultural imposition}} occurs when you consider {{c2::your own cultural values as more important}} when interacting with people of a different culture.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: Cultural imposition takes ethnocentrism to an extreme — actively forcing your values onto the patient rather than just ranking them higher.

Pitfall: The everyday form is translating a patient's behavior through your own worldview, like a North American reading an averted gaze as "hiding something" or untrustworthy.
coverage_notes: Two-way definition of the highlighted term; forced-choice hint pins the discrimination against cultural imposition.

Text: When health care providers force their own cultural values onto a patient because they believe those values are better, they are committing {{c1::cultural imposition::ethnocentrism / cultural imposition}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: Ethnocentrism stops at attitude — your own values ranked higher; imposition acts on that ranking.

Pitfall: The forcing can be conscious or subconscious — a provider may not notice doing it.
coverage_notes: Confusable sibling grounded in the same context paragraph; one-way with forced-choice discrimination hint.

Text: A physician angrily accuses parents of abuse because they treated their sick child with coining (a traditional Asian healing practice of rubbing hot coins on the back), insisting the harmless practice is dangerous. The physician's response is {{c1::cultural imposition::ethnocentrism / cultural imposition}}.
Back Extra:
Why: The physician went beyond privately ranking personal values higher — condemning the family's harmless practice as abuse forces those values onto them.

Cue: Attitude alone = ethnocentrism; forcing the attitude onto the patient = cultural imposition.
coverage_notes: Classify card; the grounded coining vignette appears ONLY here (kept off both definition siblings per check 16).

Text: A patient from Thailand has a bleeding head wound, and Thai culture reserves head-touching for {{c2::those who are very intimate::who}}. Before touching the head, you should {{c1::ask permission}}, if at all possible.
Back Extra: Why: Even during life-threatening emergencies, recognizing and respecting the patient's culture remains important.
coverage_notes: c1 = the actionable rule, c2 = the highlighted cultural fact.

Text: Facing a hostile patient, stand with your {{c1::palms facing out::hand position}} — a stance that communicates {{c2::openness}} and {{c2::acceptance}} and allows {{c2::quick movement}} if necessary.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: Crossed arms, clenched fists, or hands on hips signal impatience, disinterest, or asserted authority — the opposite message.

Pitfall: Make good eye contact with a hostile patient, but do not stare.
coverage_notes: c1 = the action, c2 = all three highlighted payoffs grouped.

Text: When a patient becomes hostile, never {{c1::threaten::action}} the patient, either verbally or physically.
Back Extra:
Why: Personal safety is your primary concern with every patient — above all one displaying hostile behavior.

Cue: Stay attentive to facial expressions, body language, and eye contact — the patient's and your own.
coverage_notes: Negation card: negator bold and visible, banned action clozed.

Text: In communication, {{c1::noise}} is {{c2::anything that dampens or obscures}} the true meaning of a message.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: Noise is broader than sound — lighting, distance, and physical obstacles all count as noise.

Distinguish: Literal noise is the subtype meaning actual environmental sounds.
coverage_notes: Two-way definition; broader-than-sound trap in Back Extra.

Text: A patient interview draws on two question types. {{c1::Open-ended::open-ended / closed-ended}} questions require the patient to {{c2::provide some level of detail}}, whereas {{c1::closed-ended::open-ended / closed-ended}} questions can be answered in {{c2::short or single-word}} responses.
Back Extra:
Ex: "What seems to be bothering you today?" — an open-ended opener when first approaching a patient.

Pitfall: Answers to closed-ended questions give limited information — treat them as a starting point only.
coverage_notes: Comparison-definition; both names under c1, both defining properties under c2. Consolidation: unflagged — the stated 'two question types' is a structural, self-verifying count, not a clinical numeric.

Text: When first approaching a patient, begin with {{c1::open-ended::open-ended / closed-ended}} questions. Switch to {{c1::closed-ended::open-ended / closed-ended}} questions when the patient is {{c2::unable to provide long or complete answers::patient state}}.
Back Extra:
Why: Open-ended questions let conversation flow freely and let the patient direct you to what is bothering them.

Ex: A patient with severe breathing trouble, or a young child, may only manage short answers.
coverage_notes: Timing/usage card for the two WHEN facts.

Text: Before beginning a patient interview, you and your partner should determine which provider will {{c1::lead::role}} the interview.
Back Extra: Why: A designated lead keeps partners from asking questions at the same time or repeating questions already asked.
coverage_notes: Single crisp cloze on the decision word.

Text: Rather than stacking an open-ended and a closed-ended question together, ask a {{c1::single}} question, {{c1::wait}} for the answer, and then proceed to another question.
Back Extra: Why: Asking two questions at once ("How are you doing today? Have you been feeling ill?") mixes the two types, and the patient often just answers "yes."
coverage_notes: Micro-sequence grouped under one cloze with crisp one-word deletions.

Text: {{c1::Facilitation}} is the therapeutic communication technique of {{c2::encouraging the patient to talk more}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: EMT: "I am listening to you. Can you tell me more about that?"

Distinguish: clarification asks what the patient meant by an answer already given; facilitation simply invites more talk.
coverage_notes: Technique 1 of 9, two-way definition; table example as Ex line.

Text: {{c1::Pause}} is the therapeutic communication technique of staying silent to give the patient {{c2::space and time to think and respond}}.
Back Extra:
Why: patients sometimes hide information, consciously or unconsciously, out of fear or confusion; quiet space lets more of the story surface.

Distinguish: facilitation invites more talk with words ("tell me more"); a pause invites it with silence.
coverage_notes: Technique 2 of 9; definition and example columns folded into one sentence.

Text: {{c1::Reflection}} is the therapeutic communication technique of restating a {{c2::statement::statement/complaint}} the patient made to you, to confirm your understanding.
Back Extra:
Ex: Patient: "I am so depressed that I could die." EMT: "I understand that you are feeling depressed."

Distinguish: interpretation restates the patient's complaint (the clinical story) for confirmation; reflection echoes a statement the patient voiced.
coverage_notes: Technique 3 of 9; c2 blanks the discriminator with forced-choice statement/complaint hint, mirrored on the Interpretation card.

Text: {{c1::Empathy}} is the therapeutic communication technique of {{c2::being sensitive to the patient's feelings and thoughts}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: eye contact, appropriate touching, and a tone of voice and pace adjusted to allow open communication.

Distinguish: reflection communicates verbally by restating the patient's words; empathy shows nonverbally, through eye contact, touch, and tone.
coverage_notes: Technique 4 of 9, two-way definition.

Text: {{c1::Clarification}} is the therapeutic communication technique of asking the patient to {{c2::explain what he or she meant by an answer}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: Patient: "I just feel sick." EMT: "Can you tell me how you are feeling sick? What feels wrong?"

Distinguish: facilitation invites more talk in general; clarification digs into the meaning of one specific answer.
coverage_notes: Technique 5 of 9, two-way definition.

Text: {{c1::Confrontation}} is the therapeutic communication technique of making a patient who is in {{c2::denial or a mental state of shock::2 states}} focus on {{c3::urgent and life-critical issues}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: a patient lists chest pain, back pain, and a medication refill all at once; EMT: "We will talk about your medicines in a moment. Please tell me about your chest pain."

Cue: the acknowledge-then-redirect shape ("in a moment... please tell me about...") is the confrontation signature.
coverage_notes: Technique 6 of 9; c1 term, c2 target population, c3 the focus.

Text: {{c1::Interpretation}} is the therapeutic communication technique of restating the patient's {{c2::complaint::statement/complaint}} to confirm your understanding.
Back Extra:
Ex: EMT: "If I understand correctly, you have been feeling pain for the past 3 days, and it has gotten worse today." Patient: "That's right."

Distinguish: reflection echoes a single statement the patient voiced (often a feeling); interpretation restates the whole complaint.
coverage_notes: Technique 7 of 9; mirror of the Reflection card with the same forced-choice discriminator.

Text: {{c1::Explanation}} is the therapeutic communication technique of providing {{c2::factual information to support a conversation}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: Patient: "I do not understand what is happening." EMT: "We have checked your blood sugar and blood pressure and don't see anything we need to immediately treat."

Distinguish: summary is the closing overview of the conversation plus the steps you will take; explanation feeds facts in mid-conversation.
coverage_notes: Technique 8 of 9, two-way definition.

Text: {{c1::Summary}} is the therapeutic communication technique of giving the patient {{c2::an overview of the conversation and the steps you will take::2 parts}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: EMT: "We will be taking you to the emergency department to care for your chest pain. I will be giving you some medication that should make you feel better."

Distinguish: explanation supplies factual information to support the conversation while it is still going; summary is the closing wrap-up.
coverage_notes: Technique 9 of 9, two-way definition with count hint on the two-part content.

Text: A patient says, "I am afraid I will never see my kids again," and the EMT replies, "You are afraid you will not see your kids again." Which therapeutic communication technique is the EMT using? {{c1::Reflection}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the EMT hands the patient's own statement back nearly word for word, adding nothing new.

Distinguish: interpretation would restate the clinical complaint ("so the pain started yesterday and is worse today"); empathy shows through eye contact, touch, and tone rather than a restatement.
coverage_notes: Classify card with fresh utterance per check 16.

Text: A patient tells you his chest feels "funny." You ask, "What do you mean by funny? What exactly does it feel like?" Which therapeutic communication technique are you using? {{c1::Clarification}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the question targets what the patient meant by an answer he already gave.

Distinguish: facilitation would be a plain invitation to keep talking ("go on, tell me more"), without probing the meaning of a specific answer.
coverage_notes: Classify card with fresh utterance per check 16.

Text: A patient bleeding heavily from one thigh keeps talking about who will feed his cat. You say, "We can sort out your cat soon. Right now, tell me about your leg." Which therapeutic communication technique are you using? {{c1::Confrontation}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the patient is avoiding the urgent problem, and the EMT acknowledges the side issue, then steers straight back to the life-critical one.

Distinguish: facilitation encourages the patient to keep talking about whatever he raises; confrontation narrows him to what is urgent.
coverage_notes: Classify card with fresh scenario per check 16.

Text:
When interviewing a patient, an EMT should avoid 8 improper interview techniques:
{{c1::giving false hope or reassurance}}
{{c1::giving unsolicited advice}}
{{c1::asking leading or biased questions}}
{{c1::talking too much}}
{{c1::interrupting the patient}}
{{c1::asking "why" questions}}
{{c1::using authoritative language}}
{{c1::speaking in professional jargon}}
Back Extra:
Why: the eight habits fall into two failure modes: disrespecting the patient (unsolicited advice, leading questions, interrupting, accusatory "why" questions, commands) and blocking real understanding (jargon, empty reassurance, talking without listening).

Ex: false reassurance sounds like "It will be okay"; authoritative language sounds like "Just give me the details."

Pitfall: reassuring words feel kind, but you do not know that everything will be okay.
coverage_notes: All 8 avoid-techniques as ONE grouped c1 list in table order. Consolidation: unflagged — the count of 8 was verified against the page 366-367 renders (structural count, no clinical numerics).

Text: During patient questioning, an EMT asks, "You're not having any trouble breathing, right?" Which improper interview technique is the EMT using? {{c1::Asking a leading or biased question}}
Back Extra:
Why: a question that suggests its own answer pressures the patient to agree rather than report; respectful interviewing lets the patient answer freely.

Distinguish: a "why" question ("Why did you wait so long to call?") sounds accusatory; a leading question plants the desired answer inside the question itself.
coverage_notes: Classify card with fresh utterance per check 16.

Text: While you care for a patient, it is generally best to keep the family {{c2::together::together/apart}}. When a family member is not helpful, consider giving him or her {{c1::a task to do}}.
Back Extra:
Why: a concrete task — gathering the patient's medications or clothing — can transform the person from a hindrance into a valuable aide.

Pitfall: separating the patient from loved ones can make the patient more anxious, so weigh asking family to step outside against keeping them close.
coverage_notes: Task-fact clozed as c1; keep-families-together baseline as c2 with forced choice.

Text: Everything an EMT does communicates something, so your {{c2::body language}} must reflect your words. People call EMS because they are in crisis — a good EMT projects {{c1::calm and control::2}} into a chaotic environment.
Back Extra:
Cue: "never let them see you sweat" — the motto for composure on scene.

Pitfall: feeling calm is not the requirement — projecting calm is; you may be stressed, but the patient should never read it on you.
coverage_notes: Project-calm fact as c1 with count hint; body-language-reflects-words as c2; the motto lives in the Cue line.

Text: You cannot make yourself understood to a hard-of-hearing patient. One clever fix is to have the patient put {{c1::a stethoscope}} in his or her ears while you {{c1::speak softly into the diaphragm}} to {{c1::amplify}} the sound.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: the diaphragm picks up your voice and the tubing pipes it straight into the patient's ears — the same acoustics used for heart and lung sounds, repurposed as a voice amplifier.

Cue: the roles are reversed — the patient wears the earpieces while you talk into the chest piece.

Why: a soft voice is all you need; the stethoscope itself provides the amplification.
coverage_notes: Parker's margin praise honored — whole trick grouped under one c1 with a rich teaching back.

Text:
Emotional intelligence — the ability to {{c2::identify, understand, and manage::3 verbs}} your own emotions and the emotions of others — improves with 4 practices:
{{c1::Assess how you react to stressful situations}}
{{c1::Practice mindfulness}}
{{c1::Take responsibility for your actions}}
{{c1::Consider how your actions will affect others}}
Back Extra:
Meaning: mindfulness = purposely focusing your attention on the current moment, without blame or judgment of yourself or others; the payoff is calm, focus, and awareness of the situation around you.

Ex: delays, tasks done incorrectly, things not going your way — minor irritations are where you practice managing frustration and keeping your composure.

Cue: the last two practices look outward — own your role rather than blaming others, and think through how your words and actions will make others feel.
coverage_notes: Lead-in highlight carded as ONE grouped c1 list of all 4 tips in source order; EI gloss folded into the stem and clozed as c2.

Text:
The behavioral change stairway model de-escalates a crisis in 5 steps, in order:
1. {{c1::Employ active listening}}
2. {{c1::Display empathy}}
3. {{c1::Build a rapport}}
4. {{c1::Exert influence}}
5. {{c1::Initiate behavior change}}
Back Extra:
Pathway: listen and acknowledge without interrupting, disagreeing, or commanding → understand the person's perspective (you need not agree or condone) → 'speak the person's language' → weigh realistic solutions that move the situation forward → propose a solution that makes sense to the person and is acceptable to you.

Why: each step builds on the previous ones, so the order cannot be skipped — the stairway climbs from listening to behavior change.
coverage_notes: Ordered grouped sequence, all 5 steps under c1. Consolidation: unflagged — page 373 render confirms the book calls it a five-step model; the fifth label (Initiate behavior change) is typeset inside item 4's paragraph, a book formatting quirk noted for the hand-off.

Text: The {{c2::behavioral change stairway model::model}} was developed by the {{c1::FBI::agency}} to manage {{c1::hostage negotiations}} quickly and effectively. The model can be adapted to most crisis communications.
Back Extra:
Cue: a stairway is climbed one step at a time — the steps are followed in order, each building on the last.

Why: the model's goal is to improve communication, build rapport, and de-escalate when emotions are running high.
coverage_notes: Name-to-origin/purpose card; c1 groups the origin story, c2 reverse-tests the model name.
